 1                  I.          INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q1.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.    My name is Rene F. Gonzalez, and my business address is 100 North Stanton Street,

4          El Paso, Texas, 79901.

5

 6   Q2.   HOW ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 7   A.    I am employed by El Paso Electric Company (“EPE” or the “Company”) as

 8         Supervisor - Rates and Regulatory.

 9

10   Q3.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY SUBMITTED TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

11   A.    Yes. I submitted Direct Testimony on August 6, 2026, in support of EPE’s

12         Amended Application for Revision of its Retail Electric Rates.

13

14   Q4.   ARE YOU SPONSORING ANY EXHIBITS IN THIS FILING?

15   A.    Yes. The exhibits I am sponsoring are listed in the table of contents to this

16         testimony.

17

18                      II.       PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

19   Q5.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

20   A.    The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to the direct testimony of

21         intervening        parties    and   New   Mexico   Public   Regulation   Commission


                                                     1
                                        EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                        REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                            RENE F. GONZALEZ

 1               (“Commission” or “NMPRC”) Advisory Staff (“Staff”) addressing the Low-

 2               Income Rider, Miscellaneous Charges, and Rate No. 11 – Street Lighting Service

 3               Rate.

 4                       My rebuttal testimony responds to the parts of the direct testimonies of

 5               NMPRC Staff witnesses Richard Bunch, Elizabeth Acosta, and Douglas Jester;

 6               Coalition for Clean Affordable Energy (“CCAE”) witness Courtney Fieldman, City

 7               of Las Cruces (“CLC”) witness Justin R. Barnes, New Mexico Department of

 8               Justice (“NMDOJ”) witness Jamal Mamkhezri, and City of Las Cruces-Dona Ana

 9               County (“CLC-DAC”) witness Mark E. Garrett that address the issues noted above.

10

11        III.       RESPONSE TO RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE LOW-INCOME

12                                                      RIDER

13   Q6.         WHAT       STAFF      AND      OR    INTERVENOR           RECOMMENDATIONS

14               REGARDING          THE     LOW-INCOME            RIDER      (“LIR”)     ARE      YOU

15               RESPONDING TO IN THIS REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

16   A.          At a high level, I am responding to questions of eligibility and reporting

17               requirements recommended regarding EPE’s Low-Income Rider proposal made by

18               Staff and Intervenors.    Specifically, Staff witness Bunch inquires about how

19               residential qualification is defined and the affect on the number of total qualified

20               customers and NMDOJ witness Mamkhezri recommends certain reporting

21               requirements, tied to the next general rate case, and states that EPE should, “finalize


                                                       2
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      RENE F. GONZALEZ

 1         its State data-sharing arrangement”.

 2            Additional questions regarding the specific reduction of the customer charge,

 3         cost recovery amongst all classes, limiting the LIR credit, and other

 4         recommendations are addressed in EPE witness Manuel Carrasco’s rebuttal

 5         testimony.

 6

 7   Q7.   PLEASE COMMENT ON THESE RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE LIR

 8         PROPOSAL.

 9   A.    Definitions used to qualify customers for the LIR, such as SNAP or LIHEAP

10         eligibility, are open as initially presented in EPE’s tariff proposal and can be

11         adjusted as appropriate. Additionally, as with any new program or pilot, EPE

12         acknowledges the need for insight into any final proposal and as such is amenable

13         to suggested reporting requirements for participation, cost, and overall

14         effectiveness of a low-income program.

15

16                 IV.    RESPONSE TO OTHER TARIFF PROPOSAL

17   Q8.   WHAT ADDITIONAL TARIFF PROPOSAL WAS MADE BY STAFF?

18   A.    Staff witness Bunch raises many concerns over Rate No. 11 – Street Lighting

19         Service Rate. Among them, as it relates to the cost of service, are the lumen output

20         of light-emitting diode (“LED”) streetlights, the costs associated with Company

21         owned LED lighting relative non-Company owned tired LED pricing, LED tariff


                                                  3
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      RENE F. GONZALEZ

 1          wattage ranges, and tariff language.

 2

 3   Q9.    DOES THE COMPANY HAVE HIGH INTENSITY DISCHARGE (“HID”)

 4          LUMINAIRES IN USE WITHIN ITS SERVICE TERRITORY?

 5   A.     Yes. As indicated on tab “WP2 – Lamp COS Ph 1” of WP O.3 Amended Filing,

 6          Excel column AM (labeled column “x”), for Rate No. 11 – Street Lighting Service

 7          Rate, EPE has approximately 1,478 HID luminaires in operation as of this filing.

 8          Additionally, within Rate No. 12 – Private Area Lighting Rate, there are an

 9          additional 5,211 HID luminaires in use.

10

11   Q10.   DO THE ABOVE FIGURES FOR HID LUMINAIRES STILL REPRESENT

12          A SIGNIFICANT PROPORTION OF IN USE INVENTORY?

13   A.     Yes.   Based on total active lamps in use, the HID luminaires represent

14          approximately 37% of active lamps for Rate No. 11, including counts for non-

15          Company owned energy only lamps, or approximately 92% without non-Company

16          owned lamps. HID luminaires also represent approximately 85% of active lamps

17          for Rate No. 12.

18

19   Q11. IS IT FAIR TO SAY THAT THE CONVERSION TO NEW LED

20          TECHNOLOGY AND THE CORRESPONDING INVESTMENT OF IN-

21          USE HID INVENTORY IS LARGELY UNREALIZED AND PENDING


                                                   4
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     RENE F. GONZALEZ

1         SIGNIFICANT CONVERSION?

2    A.   Yes.

3

4    Q12. HAS     THE       RELATIVELY          MODEST         CONVERSION           TO     LED

5         LUMINAIRES CONTRIBUTED TO AN OVERALL LOWER REVENUE

6         REQUIREMENT FOR LIGHTING AND A REDUCTION OF COSTS FOR

7         LED LUMINAIRES AND ENERGY ONLY COSTS?

8    A.   Yes. As commonly anticipated, the introduction of LED luminaires and technology

 9        represents a reduction in cost structure and energy costs when compared to older

10        HID technology.

11

12   Q13. ARE COSTS CALCULATED IN THE COST OF SERVICE (WP O.3) COST

13        BASED?

14   A.   Yes.

15

16   Q14. IS LUMEN OUTPUT A DETERMINANT AFFECTING THE COST OF

17        SERVICE FOR RATE NO. 11?

18   A.   No. While lumen output arguably has a correlation to wattage and wholesale lamp

19        costs, the cost of service does not use these criteria in the calculation of current or

20        proposed rates.

21


                                                5
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    RENE F. GONZALEZ

 1   Q15. HAS LUMEN OUTPUT SERVED ANY ADDITIONAL PURPOSE WITH

 2        RESPECT TO EPE’S OPERATIONS?

 3   A.   Yes. As lighting has evolved to include more diverse LED options, within various

 4        EPE lighting categories, the “lumen equivalency” has, likely unintentionally, been

 5        an informative guide for distinguishing between very similar LED options for

 6        Company owned lights. This has held true for the Rates, Billing, Customer Service,

 7        and the Lighting Departments, who are each charged, to varying degrees, with

 8        addressing questions and updating and maintaining the accuracy of the billing of

 9        customer accounts.

10

11   Q16. IS THERE A REASON WHY EPE DEVELOPED “TIERED” ENERGY

12        ONLY PRICING FOR NON-COMPANY OWNED LED LIGHTING?

13   A.   Yes. First, the “tiered” energy only pricing was created to accommodate known

14        manufacturing and technical differences amongst market vendor alternatives as the

15        wattage equivalency often varies from manufacturer to manufacturer. Second, the

16        demand for specific tiers of non-Company owned LED lighting was unknown and

17        a tiered pricing structure helped to accommodate this unknown without hindering

18        the number of possible customer alternatives.

19

20   Q17. WHY DOESN’T EPE HAVE A TIERED PRICING STRUCTURE FOR EPE-

21        OWNED LED LAMPS?


                                              6
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     RENE F. GONZALEZ

 1   A.   In contrast to non-Company owned lighting, EPE is in control of its own in-use

 2        inventory and knows exactly what quantity of LED lamps in each wattage range it

3         needs, helping to anticipate efficient procurement and installation needs. This fact

4         combined with the quantities previously mentioned is the practical reason why the

 5        tariff pages for the Company owned LED lights do not use the same ranges as the

 6        tariff pages for non-Company owned LED lights.

 7

 8   Q18. ARE THERE PRICING DIFFERENCES BETWEEN LED LIGHTING

 9        OPTIONS THAT APPEAR SIMILAR IN THE LIGHTING COST OF

10        SERVICE?

11   A.   Yes. Mr. Bunch’s testimony discusses LED lighting options in wattage ranges of

12        31w-50w and 51w-100w. To date, these happen to be the only LED wattage ranges

13        EPE has used to replace older, in use HID inventory. Cost information for these

14        two wattage ranges (in different categories) is largely composed of direct

15        investment/overhead costs as seen in Excel columns D-Q, and X-AF (labeled

16        columns “(a)” – “(n)”, and “(o)” – “(w)”, respectively) of WP O.3 Amended Filing.

17        Importantly, these costs are the elements differentiating Company owned and non-

18        Company (energy only) owned LED as the latter does not cause the Company to

19        incur any of these costs.

20               As for the only quantitative example used by Mr. Bunch for customer-

21        owned LED, i.e., when he refers to the pricing for a 59w ($21.95) and 89w ($25.11)


                                               7
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     RENE F. GONZALEZ

1         LED to advance the argument that EPE is using the same pricing for disparate

2         wattage ranges, two important points are required. As discussed above, EPE only

3         has two LED pricing tiers because they correspond to the only LED wattage ranges

4         in use and were developed as needed and based on known inventories of planned

5         changes unlike non-Company owned lighting, which is outside the daily purview

6         and thorough knowledge of EPE. Notably, the costs recovered in these tiers are also

7         incurred for newly proposed non-Company owned lighting when a customer

8         requests operation and maintenance by EPE beyond energy only costs, and these

 9        proposed tiers have no customers or activity in use unless EPE’s proposal is

10        approved. Secondly, and more importantly, there are no identical comparable costs

11        or Company owned pricing tiers supporting the argument that EPE is charging the

12        same prices for different wattage ranges. Admittedly, there are reasonably close

13        monthly costs included in these two LED pricing tiers though an examination of the

14        details in WP O.3 Amended Filing demonstrate some significant structural

15        differences defining these relatively similar amounts.

16

17   Q19. DO YOU HAVE ANY ADDITIONAL COMMENTS ABOUT OBSOLETE

18        LUMINAIRES,         LED    WATTAGE         RANGES,       DIFFERING       LUMEN

19        OUTPUT,       AND     OR     LAMP        CONVERSION        STANDARDS         AND

20        EQUIVALENCIES?

21   A.   Yes. As I mention in the introduction to this section of my rebuttal testimony, Mr.


                                               8
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     RENE F. GONZALEZ

 1        Bunch relays many concerns in his testimony. I address what is related to the scope

 2        of my testimony, which includes pricing and the cost of service. A thorough and

 3        additional discussion, with detailed responses to other operational concerns, can be

 4        seen in the rebuttal testimony of EPE witness Omar Gallegos.

 5               As I mentioned above, lighting options included for EPE-owned lighting

 6        and fixtures are first, limited to those that are actually in use, and second are also

 7        subject to numerous overhead costs as outlined in WP O.3 Amended Filing.

 8               EPE is attentive to modifying the lighting tariffs and the cost of service

 9        where prudent as it relates to lumen equivalency output and any needed conversion

10        language as it relates to MV to LED or HPS to LED services. The latter includes

11        any needed language for Rate No. 12 – Private Area Lighting Rate as well. EPE

12        will also review and include any new lighting tiers for Company owned LED

13        lighting to the extent lamp pricing is available and the intended use of such tiers is

14        planned and expected.

15

16                                V.      OTHER UPDATES

17   Q20. ARE THERE ANY CORRECTIONS OR ERRORS THAT WERE

18        IDENTIFIED THROUGH THE DISCOVERY AND INTERVENOR

19        DIRECT TESTIMONY PROCESS?

20   A.   Yes, Staff witness Acosta restates three errors that were correctly identified by Staff

21        for miscellaneous service charges each of which were subsequently corrected in


                                                9
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     RENE F. GONZALEZ

1         EPE’s second notice of errata filed on July 7, 2026, and carried through to EPE’s

2         Amended Application on August 6, 2026.

3                EPE identified an additional error resulting in an incorrect cost for the

4         proposed miscellaneous service charge entitled “New Service Start – Field Activity

5         Required (Standard) - (NMRCCMD).” Correcting this error revises the charge

6         initially proposed from $3.50, a significant decrease from the current charge, to

7         $19.25, which is a significant increase. This error was due to the inclusion of the

8         incorrect “function rate(s)” or minutes per function, which should have reflected

 9        that a start of new service does require field activity. Including the correct minutes

10        per function also significantly alters the total revenue anticipated and requested for

11        all miscellaneous charges from a net reduction of approximately $241,000, relative

12        to the test year revenues, to an approximately $7,000 increase.

13               Accounting for this change, with highlighted cells where revisions have

14        occurred, and included with this rebuttal testimony are a revised rebuttal Exhibit

15        RFG-1R - WP O.2.1, previously included as Exhibit E – WP O.2.1 Replacement,

16        as a part of EPE’s second notice of errata (accounting for the three errors noted just

17        above) and a revised rebuttal Exhibit RFG-2R - WP O.2.2.

18

19   Q21. ARE     THERE       ANY      ADDITIONAL          CONCERNS         RELATED         TO

20        MISCELLANEOUS CHARGES?

21   A.   Yes, CLC-DAC witness Mark E. Garrett expresses concern about $878,256 in costs


                                               10
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    RENE F. GONZALEZ

 1        incurred for meter reading expenses.

 2

 3   Q22. DO YOU HAVE ANY COMMENT ABOUT THE ABOVE COSTS FOR

 4        METER READING EXPENSE?

 5   A.   Yes. For clarity and verification, the $878,256, while correctly defined as a meter

 6        reading cost defined by FERC Account 902, is not a cost being sought for cost

 7        recovery directly from any miscellaneous charge(s).       Rather, these are total

 8        operations and maintenance (“O&M”) costs booked and requested for recovery in

 9        the Company’s overall revenue requirement and include costs that are ongoing and

10        many that are not associated with the AMS, such as the Company’s MV90 metering

11        system. The relative comparison of the $878,265 to the reduced amount of “meter”

12        costs amounting to $219,419 within WP O 2.2 Amended Filing is not an equivalent

13        like for like comparison substantiating this recommended adjustment.

14

15                                 VI.    CONCLUSION

16   Q23. DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

17   A.   Yes, it does.

18
